hours.title: Features, targets and the unit of a row
hours.outcome: Identify what each observation means and which inputs exist at prediction time.
hours.artifact: A data dictionary with units, target and prediction-time boundary.

slides.title: A row represents an observational unit
points: One row may represent a flower, device or measurement window.
Repeated measurements of one object are not automatically independent.
slides.note: Ask whether row 1 and row 2 can enter different splits. They may share device-specific information. The intended deployment population determines independence.

slides.title: A feature is an available input
points: X contains measurements available when the prediction is made.
y names the quantity or class that the model must predict.
slides.note: A feature is not simply any convenient spreadsheet column. Explain its availability and measurement process before considering predictive association.

slides.title: The target defines the question
points: Predicting temperature asks for a continuous value.
Predicting failure within seven days asks for a defined future event.
slides.note: An event horizon is part of the target definition. A vague failure label without a time window leaves the scientific question underspecified.

slides.title: Iris supplies four measured features
points: Sepal length and width describe the outer floral structures.
Petal length and width describe the petals, in centimeters.
slides.note: The botanical cover motivates measurement, not measured evidence. The dataset documentation supplies the feature names and units used in the notebook.

slides.title: A design matrix has two distinct axes
points: X has n observations and p features.
A target vector assigns one target to each supervised observation.
slides.note: This miniature table is illustrative and uses only two displayed features. Do not imply these three rows constitute the complete Iris dataset or an evaluation result.

slides.title: Shape checks protect row alignment
points: X.shape[0] must equal len(y).
A correct shape alone cannot detect shuffled or mismatched labels.
slides.visual: assert X.shape[0] == len(y)~print(X.shape, y.shape)~# Also inspect sample identities
slides.note: Ask students how the assertion can pass when y has the correct length but the wrong order. A stable row identifier supports an alignment check.

slides.title: Numbers can encode categories
points: Species IDs 0, 1 and 2 are category labels.
Their numeric differences do not define biological distances.
slides.visual: Category IDs:0  1  2,no metric distance;Measurements:1 cm  2 cm,meaningful difference
slides.note: Explain why averaging class IDs does not create a meaningful halfway species. The encoding is a representation choice rather than a physical scale.

slides.title: Identifier columns can create shortcuts
points: A serial number may reveal production batch or collection site.
High apparent prediction quality can reflect the collection process.
slides.visual: Serial ID;Batch pattern;Outcome correlation;New batch fails
slides.note: Give the example of all defective items coming from one measurement day. The ID can encode the day without representing a failure mechanism.

slides.title: Units change numerical geometry
points: Millimeters and centimeters encode the same length differently.
A distance-sensitive algorithm responds to the numeric scale.
slides.visual: Length in cm:5;Same length in mm:50
slides.note: These are the same physical quantity. The visual compares numerical values, not two different specimens. Scaling choices must respect the meaning of measurements.

slides.title: Missingness has a measurement history
points: An absent value can mean sensor failure or an unrecorded field.
Zero is a physical value and is not a universal missing-value marker.
slides.visual: Entry,Possible meaning;0,Measured zero;NaN,Not recorded;Empty,Parsing or missingness
slides.note: Ask students to describe one setting where replacing all missing values with zero reverses a scientific interpretation. Record the missingness convention explicitly.

slides.title: Imputation also learns from data
points: A median imputer estimates its replacement values from training rows.
The held-out set receives those frozen values.
slides.note: The imputer is a fitted component even though it is not the final predictor. This is the first example of preprocessing as part of the learned system.

slides.title: Availability comes before correlation
points: A repair outcome may strongly correlate with failure.
It cannot predict a failure if repair occurs after that failure.
slides.note: Draw the prediction-time boundary. The correct answer is to exclude the repair outcome for this prediction task, regardless of its apparent predictive power.

slides.title: Target leakage imports the answer
points: A post-diagnosis label proxy can make evaluation look easy.
Remove inputs unavailable at deployment or derived from the outcome.
slides.visual: Legitimate:Past sensor reading,Known before decision;Leaking:Repair verdict,Known after decision
slides.note: A strong correlation is not by itself proof of leakage. The decisive question is whether the information would exist for the real prediction being evaluated.

slides.title: Group leakage reuses object identity
points: Measurements from the same machine can share a fingerprint.
A new-machine claim requires a split that separates machines.
slides.visual: Split,Machine IDs;Train,A B C;Test,D E;Unsafe overlap,A in both
slides.note: Ask what a random-row split estimates when machines repeat. It may estimate future rows from familiar machines rather than transfer to unseen machines.

slides.title: Time leakage reuses future information
points: Forecasting must respect when each feature became available.
A random split can place later observations inside training.
slides.note: A chronological split is necessary for many forecasting claims, but preprocessing and overlapping windows also need a time-aware audit.

slides.title: One schema anchors reproducibility
points: Record column names, units, dtypes and the target meaning.
Preserve a stable identifier for tracing individual observations.
slides.note: A data dictionary is useful evidence even before fitting. It tells a second student what a row means and what information the model receives.

slides.title: Input validity differs from model accuracy
points: A model can produce a number for a physically invalid input.
Validate shape, units and allowed ranges before prediction.
slides.note: Explain that a successful API call does not establish scientific validity. A centimeter-to-meter mix-up can be accepted by software yet invalidate the inference.

slides.title: The positive class is a declared choice
points: In a binary problem, class 1 names the event of interest.
In Iris, three classes require explicit multiclass handling.
slides.visual: Binary:event versus no event,one positive class;Iris:three species,per-class interpretation
slides.note: This prepares Week 5. Do not silently apply a binary confusion-matrix formula to a three-class matrix without defining a one-versus-rest view.

slides.title: Prediction and explanation differ
points: A coefficient or importance score describes a model in context.
It does not automatically identify a causal mechanism.
slides.visual: Correlated feature;Useful prediction;Model explanation;Causal claim needs more
slides.note: Ask whether petal width causing a predicted class proves a biological intervention. The class prediction task does not justify an intervention claim.

slides.title: A thought experiment exposes a shortcut
points: Imagine recording collection date beside each flower.
Would the model still work when the collection protocol changes?
slides.visual: Same collection:Date predicts label,Shortcut looks useful;New collection:Date changes,Shortcut may fail
slides.note: Students should propose a split by collection batch or a collection-protocol stress test. The purpose is to distinguish stable evidence from a convenient association.

slides.title: A target needs an operational definition
points: Specify the event, unit and time horizon.
Two teams using different definitions are solving different tasks.
slides.visual: Task,Target definition;Quality,Pass at final inspection;Failure,Failure within 7 days;Response,Deflection in mm
slides.note: Have pairs rewrite an ambiguous target such as bad machine. Accept a definition only if another student could assign labels consistently.

slides.title: An audit can precede any model
points: List each candidate feature and its availability time.
Mark identifiers, post-outcome fields and measurement assumptions.
slides.visual: Field,Available?,Decision;Past reading,Yes,Keep;Repair cost,After event,Exclude;Device ID,Yes,Audit groups
slides.note: Emphasize that excluding a leaking feature is a design correction, not merely an attempt to lower a suspicious score.

slides.title: Explain the row before opening an AI tool
points: A prompt needs the row meaning, target and deployment condition.
A generated pipeline cannot infer missing scientific definitions reliably.
slides.visual: Task: classify flower species~Unit: one flower~Inputs: four measurements in cm~Constraint: split before fitting
slides.note: Ask what information is missing if the prompt only says improve accuracy. Students should supply the deployment condition and the evidence protocol.

slides.title: A data card states bounded claims
points: State what population the observations describe.
Record missing information instead of inventing provenance.
slides.note: Distinguish this course's teaching dataset from a deployment-ready biological study. The learner should identify at least one unknown about collection or representativeness.

slides.title: Check: which input must be rejected?
points: Predict a defect before inspection: past temperature or final inspection verdict?
Explain the availability boundary before revealing the answer.
slides.visual: Past temperature:Known before prediction;Inspection verdict:Known after prediction
slides.note: Expected answer: reject the final inspection verdict because it encodes information available only after the target-related event. Past temperature still needs validity checks.

slides.title: A defensible task fits on one page
points: Name the unit, X, y and prediction time.
Add one plausible leakage route and the test that would expose it.
slides.visual: Unit and target;Available inputs;Deployment setting;Leakage test
slides.note: This is the hour's evidence checkpoint. Collect a data dictionary and availability audit as in-class evidence, not a new weekly graded assignment.

hours.title: Splits, scaling and fitted pipelines
hours.outcome: Explain why preprocessing must learn only from the training partition.
hours.artifact: A hand-computed scaler example and a leakage-safe pipeline plan.

slides.title: Generalization concerns unseen observations
points: A training score measures performance on already fitted examples.
A held-out score asks a different question under declared sampling assumptions.
slides.visual: Training:Used for fitting,Known examples;Held-out:Excluded from fitting,New examples
slides.note: A held-out result is only as credible as its split. An apparently unseen row can still leak information through a shared object or future-derived feature.

slides.title: A test set has a single role
points: Reserve it for final evaluation of a frozen procedure.
Repeated decisions based on its score turn it into tuning data.
slides.visual: Train candidates;Choose on validation;Freeze procedure;Evaluate test
slides.note: Ask whether renaming a repeatedly consulted test set preserves independence. It does not undo adaptive reuse of the same evidence.

slides.title: Validation supports model choices
points: Use validation to choose settings and decision rules.
Keep the test labels outside the selection loop.
slides.note: Model selection includes preprocessing choices and feature engineering, not only estimator hyperparameters. Each selection step consumes evidence.

slides.title: The split follows the claim
points: Independent objects may support an IID split.
Grouped or temporal deployment needs corresponding separation.
slides.visual: Claim,Split unit;New independent flowers,Rows under IID assumption;New machines,Machine groups;Future readings,Time order
slides.note: No single split is universally correct. Ask students to connect a concrete deployment scenario to the unit that must remain unseen.

slides.title: Stratification preserves class proportions
points: It allocates class members across partitions approximately proportionally.
It does not remove group leakage or time leakage.
slides.visual: Stratification:Balances label counts;Group split:Separates entity identity
slides.note: Students often treat stratification as a universal safeguard. Clarify the separate purposes of class balance and independence.

slides.title: A seed freezes one random choice
points: Reusing a seed can reproduce a particular split.
A seed alone does not freeze data order, software or hardware behavior.
slides.note: Explain why a newly sorted CSV can change an index-based split even with the same seed. Saving identities makes the split auditable.

slides.title: A scaler estimates two statistics
points: Standardization uses training mean and training standard deviation.
Held-out data must use those same stored parameters.
slides.visual: z = (x - mu_train) / sigma_train;fit: learn mu and sigma;transform: reuse them
slides.note: StandardScaler uses population variance with ddof=0. Avoid confusing its scaling convention with the sample covariance convention used in PCA derivations.

slides.title: Mean from three training values
points: Training values 2, 4 and 6 have mean 4.
Squared deviations sum to 8.
slides.note: Compute the mean aloud before using a library. These are deliberately synthetic one-feature training observations.

slides.title: Standard deviation sets the scale
points: Population variance is 8/3.
The standard deviation is sqrt(8/3), approximately 1.633.
slides.note: Ask why the denominator is 3 rather than 2 in this StandardScaler teaching example. Relate it to ddof=0 rather than a universal definition of variance.

slides.title: A held-out extreme stays extreme
points: A held-out value 100 uses mean 4 and standard deviation 1.633.
Its standardized value is about 58.79.
slides.note: A large z-score is not a reason to refit the scaler on the test point. It can signal shift or an unusual observation that deserves investigation.

slides.title: Full-data scaling changes the question
points: Adding the test value to fitting changes the mean to 28.
The representation now depends on a supposedly unseen observation.
slides.note: Use the live toggle to compare training-only statistics with full-data statistics. The leakage is in the protocol, not in whether one version earns a better score.

slides.title: Fit and transform are distinct operations
points: fit estimates parameters from the supplied data.
transform applies already estimated parameters to new observations.
slides.visual: fit:Training rows,Learn statistics;transform:New rows,Use frozen statistics
slides.note: Ask students to name three fitted preprocessing operations: standardization, imputation and PCA are valid examples.

slides.title: A pipeline includes preprocessing
points: A classifier receives the scaler's transformed output.
Fitting the pipeline fits each stage using training rows.
slides.note: Trace the data through the pipeline. Do not imply the classifier directly sees the raw centimeter measurements after a scaling stage.

slides.title: Prediction reuses the fitted stages
points: New rows pass through the stored scaler.
The classifier predicts without retraining the pipeline.
slides.note: The prediction path is different from the fitting path. Ask students which parameters change during predict: none should be refitted.

slides.title: Cross-validation needs an inner pipeline
points: Each fold learns its own preprocessing from that fold's training rows.
A global scaler fitted before CV can leak validation-fold information.
slides.visual: Fold,Fit preprocessing on;1,Other folds only;2,Other folds only;3,Other folds only
slides.note: The pipeline must sit inside cross-validation. Preprocessing the entire dataset first and then passing transformed data into CV does not preserve this separation.

slides.title: Open the Week 2 notebook
points: Use CPU Colab or a Python 3 Jupyter kernel.
Run the setup cell before inspecting the Iris dataset.
slides.visual: Notebook: week-02-practice.ipynb~Runtime: Python 3 / CPU~First action: setup cell
slides.note: Guided practice begins here, after 30 minutes of theory. The notebook uses free local packages and requires no paid model API.

slides.title: Environment identity belongs in evidence
points: Record the actual Python and package versions.
Keep SEED fixed for the first run.
slides.visual: Evidence,Why;Python version,Runtime identity;Package versions,Implementation identity;Seed,Random choice
slides.note: Do not copy a version number from the lecture. Students must record their runtime's actual values.

slides.title: Inspect the full feature matrix
points: Identify the observation and feature axes.
Match feature names to their documented units.
slides.note: Iris contains 150 observations and four input measurements. Class-name order must come from the loaded object rather than a guessed mapping.

slides.title: Separate inputs from labels
points: X carries measurements and y carries species IDs.
Check alignment before creating partitions.
slides.visual: Dataset object;X measurements;y species IDs;Aligned rows
slides.note: A successful model fit cannot prove that labels were aligned correctly. Trace one sample from its original position to its partition if needed.

slides.title: Inspect the split before fitting
points: Print the train and test sizes and class counts.
Explain what deployment condition this split approximates.
slides.visual: print(X_train.shape, X_test.shape)~# Inspect class counts in each split~# Explain the independence assumption
slides.note: Do not impose a new split ratio on an already supplied notebook. Students should inspect and record the actual ratio used by their notebook.

slides.title: Read the pipeline left to right
points: The first learned stage transforms measurements.
The final learned stage maps transformed inputs to class predictions.
slides.note: Use the notebook's actual variable names. The mechanism is the teaching target, so students should explain each stage before asking AI to rewrite it.

slides.title: Fit with training labels only
points: The estimator learns from training examples and their targets.
Test features and test labels must not influence fit.
slides.note: Ask what changes if X_test is accidentally passed into fit. A completed execution would still be possible while the evaluation protocol becomes invalid.

slides.title: A fitted scaler exposes its statistics
points: Inspect the scaler's stored mean and scale.
Compare them with statistics computed from training rows.
slides.note: Do not expect the standardized test set to have exactly mean zero. Only the fitted training statistics impose that property on the training transform.

slides.title: A safe change has a prediction
points: Before changing one setting, state the expected effect.
Preserve the original split and evidence record.
slides.visual: Before:One expected effect,Original evidence;After:One changed setting,Observed difference
slides.note: Students may predict no clear improvement. The purpose is a controlled comparison, not a search for a preferred score.

slides.title: Check: where does scaling belong?
points: Choose between scaling before the split and fitting a pipeline after the split.
Explain the information boundary rather than naming a preferred function.
slides.visual: Unsafe:Fit scaler on all X,Then split;Safe:Split raw X,Fit pipeline on train
slides.note: Expected answer: the second protocol. The explanation should name which held-out information would otherwise influence the fitted representation.

slides.title: Save the intermediate checkpoint
points: Preserve the split description and fitted-pipeline configuration.
H3 will evaluate errors and export the evidence record.
slides.visual: Split description;Pipeline parameters;Observed predictions;Resume in H3
slides.note: The checkpoint can be a saved notebook state and a short written protocol. Runtime memory alone is temporary, especially in Colab.

hours.title: Pipeline lab and error inspection
hours.outcome: Run the supplied classification pipeline and explain its limited evidence.
hours.artifact: Executed notebook, evidence JSON and a claim with a limitation.

slides.title: The lab has three outputs
points: Keep an executed notebook and its evidence JSON.
Add a short claim, evidence and limitation statement.
slides.note: State the completion criterion before coding. These are in-class practice artifacts, not an additional weekly graded assignment.

slides.title: Restore the H2 checkpoint
points: Confirm the same dataset, split and pipeline configuration.
Restart from the setup cell if the runtime lost its state.
slides.visual: Open notebook;Check configuration;Restore or restart;Continue in order
slides.note: A restored browser tab does not guarantee a restored Python kernel. Students should distinguish the document from the runtime.

slides.title: A fresh run exposes hidden state
points: Restart the kernel and run cells from top to bottom.
Resolve missing variables by restoring execution order.
slides.visual: Restart kernel~Run all cells in order~Record the first failing cell
slides.note: Do not keep adding cells that depend on stale variables. A linear rerun is the evidence that another student can follow the notebook.

slides.title: Check inputs before predictions
points: Confirm row alignment, feature order and units.
Inspect the class mapping rather than guessing label meanings.
slides.visual: Check,Expected evidence;Rows,X and y align;Features,Documented order;Targets,Known class names
slides.note: Ask students to explain why permuting feature columns can change predictions even though the shape remains unchanged.

slides.title: Record the actual partition
points: Write down train and test counts from this run.
State whether this is an IID, group or temporal evaluation.
slides.visual: Partition,Record from run;Training,Actual count;Test,Actual count;Assumption,Independent flowers
slides.note: Counts must come from the executed notebook. Do not substitute a lecture's illustrative partition for the notebook's actual configuration.

slides.title: Fit the complete pipeline
points: Fit preprocessing and classification together on training data.
Predict on the unchanged held-out feature matrix.
slides.note: Use the provided notebook's variable names if they differ. The intended invariant is that held-out observations never enter fitting.

slides.title: Accuracy counts correct classifications
points: Accuracy is correct predictions divided by test observations.
Report the test size beside the score.
slides.note: This ten-observation calculation is a synthetic worked example. It is not the notebook's measured result.

slides.title: A three-class matrix preserves error types
points: Rows represent true classes and columns predicted classes.
The diagonal contains correct predictions.
slides.visual: True / Pred,Class A,Class B,Class C;Class A,4,0,0;Class B,0,3,1;Class C,0,1,3
slides.note: This illustrative matrix contains 12 observations and 10 correct predictions. Students must compare the pattern with their actual matrix rather than copy these counts.

slides.title: Off-diagonal entries name confusions
points: True B predicted C differs from true C predicted B.
Describe each error direction in words.
slides.visual: B to C:True B,Predicted C;C to B:True C,Predicted B
slides.note: A confusion matrix is an accounting device. The cell's meaning requires reading both axes, not just locating a colored square.

slides.title: Inspect one wrong prediction
points: Find a test position where prediction differs from truth.
Inspect its feature values and class mapping.
slides.visual: wrong = np.flatnonzero(pred != y_test)~print(wrong)~# Inspect one position if available
slides.note: The notebook may have few or no wrong predictions for a particular split. Never invent an error case simply to satisfy a worksheet.

slides.title: Zero observed errors has a limit
points: A small held-out sample can miss important failure modes.
Zero errors in this test does not prove zero deployment risk.
slides.visual: Observed:No errors in this sample;Unproven:No errors in all future data
slides.note: Have students name a population shift that the teaching dataset does not cover. The limitation belongs beside the result.

slides.title: A row position is not always an identity
points: A test-array position refers to the reordered test matrix.
Preserve original sample IDs if exact traceability matters.
slides.visual: Original sample ID;Split index mapping;Test-array position;Error inspection
slides.note: Explain how index 0 in X_test can refer to a different original sample. Students should not confuse local array position with dataset identity.

slides.title: The confusion matrix fixes a denominator
points: The diagonal sum divided by all cells equals accuracy.
Compare this calculation with the library result.
slides.visual: accuracy = diagonal sum / total;worked matrix: 10 / 12;accuracy = 0.8333 approximately
slides.note: This analytic consistency check uses the worked matrix shown earlier, not a claimed notebook outcome.

slides.title: A comparison changes one factor
points: Keep the partition and evaluation rule fixed.
Change only the specified model setting or feature treatment.
slides.visual: Fixed data;Fixed split;One changed factor;Comparable result
slides.note: If several changes occur simultaneously, a score difference cannot identify which change caused it. Require a written before-and-after configuration.

slides.title: Prediction comes before execution
points: Write whether the change should help, hurt or remain uncertain.
State the mechanism behind that prediction.
slides.note: Uncertain is acceptable if accompanied by a reason. This exercise trains experimental reasoning rather than hindsight storytelling.

slides.title: Keep the baseline evidence
points: Save the first run before making a change.
Use separate filenames or explicit run identifiers.
slides.note: Students should be able to recover both runs. Overwriting the only JSON file can erase the comparison they are asked to explain.

slides.title: Scaling is not an automatic improvement
points: Its effect depends on the estimator and optimization.
A safe protocol can yield the same or a different score.
slides.visual: Protocol quality:Training-only fit;Measured outcome:Observed held-out score
slides.note: Do not promise a score increase from StandardScaler. The lesson is the information boundary and the geometry, not a universal performance claim.

slides.title: A result needs a population statement
points: Describe which observations the held-out sample represents.
Avoid extending an Iris result to arbitrary biological diagnosis.
slides.note: Ask each pair to write one supported statement and one unsupported extrapolation from the same result.

slides.title: Export the evidence JSON
points: Save the seed, actual versions and measured summary.
Inspect the filename and download it before leaving Colab.
slides.visual: record = {"seed": SEED, "result": summary}~# Use the notebook export cell~# Download artifacts/
slides.note: Colab runtime storage is temporary. A printed JSON object is useful for inspection but does not replace downloading the file.

slides.title: Check the exported record
points: Match each reported count or metric to the run output.
Confirm that the record identifies this experiment.
slides.visual: Field,Check;Seed,Matches configuration;Metric,Matches observed output;Run ID,Distinguishes comparison
slides.note: This is a provenance check rather than another model search. Students must not revise a JSON score by hand to make it match an expected lecture example.

slides.title: A screenshot cannot rerun a pipeline
points: Preserve code, configuration and data identity.
Use screenshots only as supplementary visual evidence.
slides.visual: Screenshot:Shows one visible output;Notebook plus metadata:Supports a rerun
slides.note: Ask what happens if the screenshot omits the split seed or feature order. The missing information prevents a faithful reproduction.

slides.title: A peer rerun tests the instructions
points: Exchange the notebook and stated configuration.
Compare the protocol before comparing scores.
slides.visual: Partner opens;Fresh runtime;Run in order;Compare evidence
slides.note: If the runs differ, first inspect data identity, versions, split and configuration. Do not assume every difference means a conceptual failure.

slides.title: Explain one model decision cautiously
points: Connect an error to measured features and class overlap.
Distinguish an observation from a causal explanation.
slides.visual: Observation:Similar feature values;Hypothesis:Overlap may explain error
slides.note: A plausible post-hoc story is not established causation. Suggest a targeted inspection or additional measurement that could challenge the story.

slides.title: AI assistance needs a bounded request
points: Ask for an explanation of one pipeline stage or error.
Verify suggested changes against the frozen evaluation protocol.
slides.visual: Explain this scaler step.~Do not change the split or target.~List assumptions before suggesting code.
slides.note: Students remain responsible for the task definition and evidence. A fluent explanation can still suggest a leaking preprocessing change.

slides.title: Pair check: defend the pipeline
points: Name what fit learns and what predict reuses.
Explain one reason the score may fail to transfer.
slides.note: A complete explanation names both preprocessing and estimator parameters. It also states a concrete population or measurement limitation.

slides.title: Package a bounded result
points: Report the actual score and the test count.
Attach one inspected error or a stated no-error limitation.
slides.visual: Claim,Measured on held-out sample;Evidence,Notebook and JSON;Limit,Sampling or shift;Next test,Concrete stress case
slides.note: The final checkpoint should be short enough to explain orally. It prepares students for the written and oral assessments without adding an unannounced weekly assignment.

hours.title: Regression, loss and baselines
hours.outcome: Compute a linear prediction and distinguish a fitted model from a meaningful baseline.
hours.artifact: A worked regression calculation and a baseline comparison plan.

slides.title: Supervision supplies example answers
points: Each training input has an associated target.
Fitting chooses parameters to reduce a declared training objective.
slides.note: Supervised learning uses examples rather than a programmer writing every input-output rule. The objective still reflects human choices about the task and error cost.

slides.title: Regression predicts a continuous quantity
points: A response such as displacement has numerical units.
Its errors should be interpreted in those same task units.
slides.visual: Regression:Deflection in mm,Continuous output;Classification:Pass or fail,Category output
slides.note: Ask which target preserves more information. Converting a continuous target to a category changes the question and discards magnitude information.

slides.title: A linear model combines feature effects
points: y_hat equals an intercept plus weighted input features.
Linearity concerns the coefficients in this representation.
slides.visual: y_hat = b + w1*x1 + w2*x2;One coefficient per feature
slides.note: A linear model can use transformed features such as x squared while remaining linear in the coefficients. Separate linear in parameters from a straight line in raw input space.

slides.title: The intercept establishes the reference
points: b is the prediction when all represented inputs equal zero.
That reference may lie outside the observed input range.
slides.note: A mathematical intercept need not have a useful physical interpretation if zero inputs are unobserved or the features are standardized.

slides.title: A coefficient has conditional meaning
points: w1 describes the prediction change per unit of x1 while other inputs stay fixed.
Correlated features can make this interpretation unstable.
slides.visual: change in y_hat = w1 * change in x1;Other represented features held fixed
slides.note: Stress that the statement describes the fitted model, not a causal intervention on the physical system.

slides.title: Compute one prediction by hand
points: Let b=1, w1=3 and w2=-2.
For x1=2 and x2=1, the prediction is 5.
slides.note: Ask students to identify the units implied by each coefficient. A coefficient's magnitude cannot be compared across differently scaled features without care.

slides.title: A residual retains its sign
points: Define residual r as observed minus predicted.
A positive residual means the model underpredicted this observation.
slides.note: Use the sign convention consistently. Some software or plots use prediction minus observation, so students must read the definition rather than assume a universal sign.

slides.title: Absolute error measures distance
points: If y=7 and y_hat=5, absolute error is 2.
MAE averages these absolute differences.
slides.note: Absolute error returns the target unit. It does not indicate whether the model consistently predicts too high or too low.

slides.title: Squared error emphasizes large misses
points: Residuals 1 and 3 produce squares 1 and 9.
MSE uses squared target units.
slides.visual: Squared error for residual 1:1;Squared error for residual 3:9
slides.note: Compare the relative contribution under absolute and squared losses. The larger miss matters three times under absolute error and nine times under squared error.

slides.title: RMSE restores the target unit
points: RMSE is the square root of MSE.
It retains the stronger influence of large errors.
slides.note: Avoid claiming RMSE and MAE are interchangeable. They respond differently to the residual distribution and must match the decision context.

slides.title: Loss defines the fitting problem
points: Ordinary least squares minimizes the sum of squared training residuals.
Minimizing training loss does not directly minimize future error.
slides.visual: SSE = sum((y_i - y_hat_i)^2);Choose weights that minimize SSE
slides.note: Ask what evidence connects low training SSE with useful future predictions. Students should name held-out evaluation and the assumptions behind the split.

slides.title: A baseline makes improvement meaningful
points: A constant predictor ignores the features.
A fitted model should justify its added complexity against that reference.
slides.visual: Constant baseline;Feature-based model;Same held-out rows;Compare errors
slides.note: Comparing scores on different test samples or different targets confounds the interpretation. Both candidates need a shared evaluation protocol.

slides.title: The mean minimizes squared error
points: For a constant predictor under squared loss, the training mean is optimal.
Compute it from training targets only.
slides.visual: c_mean = mean(y_train);Predict c_mean for every test row
slides.note: This is the default constant strategy in the supplied DummyRegressor. Its fit stage still uses targets and must exclude held-out outcomes.

slides.title: The median minimizes absolute error
points: Under absolute loss, a training median is an optimal constant.
The notebook's mean baseline is valid but not MAE-optimal by definition.
slides.note: This distinction prevents a subtle overclaim. Students may add a median baseline as a clearly declared extension rather than silently rewriting the provided baseline.

slides.title: A baseline example is fully calculable
points: Training targets 1, 2 and 9 have mean 4 and median 2.
Compare both constants on these three targets.
slides.note: Compute absolute errors: mean gives 3+2+5=10; median gives 1+0+7=8. Squared sums are 9+4+25=38 and 1+0+49=50.

slides.title: Fitting is an optimization step
points: A parameter update should reduce the chosen objective locally.
A stopping condition and numerical scale affect the computation.
slides.note: The objective curve is a schematic, not a record of a model training run. Distinguish mathematical optimization behavior from measured learning curves.

slides.title: A gradient gives local sensitivity
points: The derivative states how loss changes for a small parameter change.
Gradient descent moves against the gradient.
slides.visual: w_next = w - eta * gradient;eta is the learning rate
slides.note: Explain the sign with a one-dimensional bowl. The minus sign aims downhill for a sufficiently small step, not for every possible step size.

slides.title: A quadratic example exposes the update
points: For L(w)=(w-3)^2, the derivative is 2(w-3).
From w=0 with eta=0.1, the next value is 0.6.
slides.note: Ask whether one update reaches the minimum. It does not. The calculation explains a step rather than asserting convergence after a single iteration.

slides.title: A large step can overshoot
points: The local downhill direction does not guarantee a safe step length.
Compare moderate and excessive learning rates on the same bowl.
slides.note: Use a schematic with an overshooting update. The failure concerns optimization settings, which differ from the statistical problem of overfitting.

slides.title: More flexible models can fit noise
points: Additional flexibility may reduce training residuals.
Held-out error determines whether the flexibility helps the intended task.
slides.note: The drawn curves are schematic and explicitly labeled. Do not present them as actual polynomial-model training outcomes.

slides.title: Noise limits exact recovery
points: The supplied generator adds random noise to a linear mechanism.
Even a correctly specified model need not predict every observed target exactly.
slides.note: These are the actual generative coefficients and noise scale used in Week 3. The third feature has zero generating coefficient.

slides.title: An irrelevant feature can acquire a weight
points: Finite samples can correlate an unused feature with the target.
A nonzero fitted weight is not proof of a physical effect.
slides.visual: Generating coefficient:Third feature = 0;Fitted coefficient:May differ from 0
slides.note: Ask students which evidence would distinguish a stable relationship from a sample-specific coefficient. Suggest resampling, new data and domain knowledge.

slides.title: Prediction quality and parameter recovery differ
points: A model can predict well while coefficients vary among correlated inputs.
Evaluate predictions and interpretation as separate claims.
slides.note: The supplied generator helps compare learned and known coefficients. Real observational data rarely provide known generating coefficients.

slides.title: A model comparison needs fixed units
points: MAE values are comparable only for a shared target and scale.
A Celsius error and a millimeter error cannot be ranked as model quality.
slides.visual: Comparable:Same target,Same held-out rows;Not comparable:Different units,Different tasks
slides.note: Students should resist declaring a classifier better than a regressor because its numeric score is larger. Metrics encode different questions.

slides.title: Check: which baseline fits the loss?
points: For constant prediction, choose mean for squared loss and median for absolute loss.
Explain why a valid baseline can still be improvable.
slides.visual: Mean:Minimizes training SSE;Median:Minimizes training absolute loss
slides.note: Expected answer should include the training-only restriction. Neither result automatically identifies the best constant on future samples.

slides.title: The first evidence comparison is ready
points: Declare the regression target, baseline and MAE.
Predict whether the feature-based model should improve on the baseline.
slides.note: A directional expectation is reasonable for this known synthetic signal, but the class must report actual measured values rather than a promised performance number.

hours.title: Ridge, probabilities and classification
hours.outcome: Trace regularization and explain how a score becomes a class decision.
hours.artifact: A ridge calculation and a guided two-task notebook comparison.

slides.title: Ridge adds a weight penalty
points: The objective combines squared residuals and a penalty on coefficient size.
The intercept is normally unpenalized in this formulation.
slides.note: This matches scikit-learn Ridge's unnormalized squared-residual objective. Avoid silently adding a factor of n that would change the interpretation of alpha.

slides.title: Alpha controls shrinkage strength
points: Larger alpha discourages large coefficients more strongly.
The best choice depends on validation under the intended task.
slides.note: A larger penalty is not universally better. It can stabilize estimates while increasing bias and potentially worsening held-out error.

slides.title: A centered example has a closed form
points: Use x values -2,-1,0,1,2 and y=3x+1.
The centered sums are Sxx=10 and Sxy=30.
slides.note: The mean of x is zero and mean of y is one. These exact synthetic observations support a hand-calculated one-feature ridge solution.

slides.title: Ridge shrinks an exact slope
points: The slope is 30/(10+alpha), with intercept 1.
At alpha=10, the slope becomes 1.5.
slides.note: Derive the formula by setting the derivative of SSE plus alpha times w squared to zero after centering.

slides.title: Explore the penalty live
points: Move alpha and inspect the fitted slope and residual sum.
Compare the data-fit term with the penalized objective.
slides.note: The demo solves the analytic example, not the supplied notebook's three-feature dataset. Ask students to predict slope direction before moving the slider.

slides.title: Regularization changes interpretation
points: Shrunk coefficients depend on feature scaling and penalty strength.
A small coefficient can reflect the penalty as well as weak evidence.
slides.note: This is why reporting coefficients without preprocessing and alpha can be misleading. Do not interpret magnitude as a universal physical importance measure.

slides.title: Classification changes the target
points: The notebook defines class 1 by y greater than zero.
The resulting event is a category, not a response magnitude.
slides.visual: label = 1 if y > 0 else 0;Class 1 means positive response
slides.note: Since y includes noise, the boundary includes label uncertainty. A response of 0.1 and a response of 10 share the same binary label but different magnitudes.

slides.title: Logistic regression starts with a score
points: A weighted sum produces a real-valued score z.
A sigmoid maps the binary score into the interval from zero to one.
slides.visual: z = b + w dot x;p = 1 / (1 + exp(-z))
slides.note: This slide discusses binary logistic regression. The Week 2 multiclass Iris model needs the appropriate multiclass probability handling rather than this single-sigmoid formula.

slides.title: The sigmoid is monotone
points: At z=0, the sigmoid equals 0.5.
Larger scores produce larger model probabilities.
slides.note: A numerical probability output is a model estimate. Calibration requires separate empirical checking and is not guaranteed by using a sigmoid.

slides.title: Cross-entropy fits probability scores
points: A confident wrong prediction incurs a large logarithmic loss.
Classification accuracy does not directly describe this fitting objective.
slides.note: For y=1, p=0.9 gives a much smaller loss than p=0.1. Clipping or numerical stabilization is an implementation matter, not permission to ignore impossible log values.

slides.title: A threshold creates the decision
points: Predict class 1 when the estimated probability is at least tau.
The same fitted scores can support different decision thresholds.
slides.visual: predicted class = 1 if p >= tau;Common reference threshold: tau = 0.5
slides.note: Changing the threshold does not retrain the underlying logistic coefficients. Week 5 studies how to choose the threshold without using test labels.

slides.title: A probability is not a physical unit
points: A classifier's score estimates an event under its modeling assumptions.
A regressor predicts the original response scale.
slides.visual: Regression output:Response units;Classifier output:Event probability estimate
slides.note: A probability of 0.8 is not the same as a predicted response of 0.8. Students should explain what random variable each output concerns.

slides.title: Accuracy hides response magnitude
points: A near-zero target and an extreme target can count as one correct class each.
Classification discards distinctions retained by regression.
slides.note: Ask what decision would require the original magnitude. This motivates selecting a task from the decision rather than choosing a familiar algorithm first.

slides.title: A model score can be miscalibrated
points: Predicted probability and observed event frequency may disagree.
Good ranking does not establish accurate probability estimates.
slides.visual: Ranking:Order cases by score;Calibration:Compare score with event frequency
slides.note: This is a conceptual preview, not a claim about the supplied logistic model's measured calibration. Do not infer calibration from classification accuracy.

slides.title: Compare tasks without ranking unlike metrics
points: Regression MAE and classification accuracy answer different questions.
Report each with its target and partition.
slides.note: The notebook creates separate stratified and unstratified splits for its two tasks. Their results are not a same-test-set head-to-head ranking of unlike metrics.

slides.title: Open the Week 3 notebook
points: The dataset has 240 rows and three synthetic inputs.
The target follows the stated linear mechanism plus noise.
slides.note: Guided practice starts after the first 30 minutes. Do not treat synthetic data as an observed engineering dataset.

slides.title: Inspect the generating mechanism
points: The first two true coefficients are 3 and -2.
The third feature contributes no term to the generating rule.
slides.visual: True coefficient x1:3;True coefficient x2:-2;True coefficient x3:0
slides.note: A bar chart with negative values must show the zero reference and both signs. This is a known teaching mechanism, not a recovered experimental law.

slides.title: The regression split reserves 60 rows
points: The notebook uses 25 percent of 240 rows for testing.
Fit the baseline and Ridge on the same 180 training rows.
slides.note: These counts follow the supplied notebook. Both regression candidates must share the same test observations for a meaningful MAE comparison.

slides.title: Fit the mean baseline first
points: DummyRegressor uses training targets to learn a constant.
Predict the held-out responses and compute MAE.
slides.note: The default strategy is mean. Explain why this establishes a valid reference but not the minimum-MAE constant baseline in every sample.

slides.title: Fit Ridge with the declared alpha
points: The supplied regression uses alpha=1.
Preserve the baseline and split while fitting the feature model.
slides.note: Do not change alpha after viewing test errors and still describe the test as untouched. Any tuning extension needs a validation protocol.

slides.title: Report the two observed MAEs
points: Compare actual values from the same held-out targets.
Do not copy a predicted or previously observed score.
slides.visual: Candidate,Record this run;Mean baseline,Observed test MAE;Ridge alpha 1,Observed test MAE
slides.note: Ask whether a lower Ridge MAE supports a claim about arbitrary real engineering data. It supports only this synthetic task and declared sampling setup.

slides.title: Build the classification target
points: Convert the generated response into the event y greater than zero.
Inspect class counts before the stratified split.
slides.visual: labels = (y > 0).astype(int)~# Inspect counts and class meaning
slides.note: The labels reuse the generated responses but represent a different supervised task. The code's event definition is part of the experiment record.

slides.title: Fit the binary classifier
points: Fit logistic regression on the classification training partition.
Extract the probability column for the declared positive class.
slides.note: The positive-column interpretation relies on the class order. Confirm classes_ if the label encoding changes.

slides.title: Apply a declared reference threshold
points: Classify with probability at least 0.5 in this notebook.
Compute accuracy against bte, not the regression targets.
slides.note: A common implementation error compares predictions with a mismatched target array from the regression task. Shapes alone may not catch every alignment problem.

slides.title: A prediction plot shows structure
points: Plot held-out observed responses against predicted responses.
The diagonal denotes perfect agreement on matching axes.
slides.note: This lecture graphic is a schematic. The student's notebook plot must contain the actual held-out outputs from their run.

slides.title: Save a two-task checkpoint
points: Record the two target definitions and their metrics.
H3 will inspect residuals, coefficients and limitations.
slides.note: Preserve which split belongs to which task. A single unlabeled score table is insufficient to reproduce both experiments.

hours.title: Regression and classification lab
hours.outcome: Compare a baseline, inspect residuals and explain what the fitted coefficients support.
hours.artifact: Executed two-task notebook, evidence JSON and a coefficient interpretation.

slides.title: Restore both task definitions
points: Regression predicts the synthetic continuous response.
Classification predicts whether that response exceeds zero.
slides.note: Begin by asking students to say both targets aloud. This guards against treating the two tasks as interchangeable model choices.

slides.title: Rebuild the environment
points: Run setup before generating data or fitting estimators.
Keep the first run's seed and generator unchanged.
slides.note: The random generator's state depends on execution order. Restarting and running all is more reliable than rerunning isolated generation cells.

slides.title: Inspect all three inputs
points: Confirm X has 240 rows and three feature columns.
Check that y contains one continuous response per row.
slides.note: The expectation refers to this notebook's construction, not a universal regression requirement. A mismatch means stop before fitting.

slides.title: Preserve the regression partition
points: Confirm 180 training rows and 60 held-out rows.
Use that exact partition for both regression candidates.
slides.note: A fair comparison holds the evaluation cases fixed. Repeatedly resplitting until a desired winner appears consumes the test evidence.

slides.title: Reproduce the baseline output
points: Identify the training mean that DummyRegressor predicts.
Check that test predictions are constant.
slides.visual: baseline.predict(Xte)[:5]~# All equal the learned training constant
slides.note: Ask why the baseline can still have a fit method despite ignoring X. It learns its constant from training targets.

slides.title: Fit and inspect Ridge
points: Confirm alpha=1 for the supplied run.
Read the intercept and three learned coefficients.
slides.note: The learned values should be reported as observed. They need not exactly equal 0, 3, -2 and 0 because of noise, finite samples and shrinkage.

slides.title: Compare MAE on a shared test set
points: Lower MAE means smaller average absolute response error here.
Include the target definition and n=60.
slides.visual: Report field,Value source;Target,Generator definition;Test count,60;Baseline MAE,Actual run;Ridge MAE,Actual run
slides.note: The slide deliberately leaves measured MAEs to the learner's run. No fabricated training output should enter the lecture's evidence table.

slides.title: Compute a tiny MAE independently
points: For observed [1,3,5] and predicted [2,2,4], errors are [1,1,1].
The MAE is 1 target unit.
slides.note: This worked example verifies the metric convention without relying on a library call. It is separate from the 60-row notebook test.

slides.title: Trace the prediction diagonal
points: Equal axis values lie on the perfect-prediction reference.
Points above the diagonal indicate overprediction.
slides.note: This uses observed values on the horizontal axis and predictions vertically. Reverse-axis plots require a correspondingly different reading.

slides.title: Residuals need a sign convention
points: Compute r=y_test-prediction.
Positive values indicate underprediction with this definition.
slides.note: Students should be able to explain the sign of one actual residual. Do not assume the sign convention from another plot or software package.

slides.title: Residual plots reveal systematic patterns
points: Plot residuals against predictions or a selected feature.
Curvature can suggest a missing relationship.
slides.note: A pattern suggests a diagnostic hypothesis, not proof of its cause. The supplied linear generator may show mostly noise rather than curvature.

slides.title: The largest error deserves inspection
points: Locate the largest absolute residual.
Inspect its inputs, observed response and prediction together.
slides.note: One extreme case can expose a data problem, an unusual input or ordinary noise. Avoid deleting it merely because it worsens a score.

slides.title: Known coefficients support a teaching check
points: Compare learned weights with [3,-2,0].
Describe the difference without demanding exact equality.
slides.note: The known mechanism is a special advantage of synthetic teaching data. Real-world interpretation usually needs additional evidence beyond a fitted coefficient.

slides.title: A coefficient can depend on scale
points: Multiplying one input by 100 changes its numerical coefficient.
Predictions can remain equivalent after a corresponding transformation.
slides.note: With regularization, changing scale can also change the fitted solution unless the preprocessing and penalty are handled appropriately.

slides.title: Declare an alpha experiment first
points: Choose a small predefined set of candidate alpha values.
Use a new training-only validation split for selection.
slides.visual: Training partition;Inner validation;Choose alpha;Final test once
slides.note: This is an optional extension beyond the supplied fixed-alpha run. Do not use the existing final test to select the best alpha.

slides.title: A median baseline is an extension
points: Add DummyRegressor(strategy='median') under the same regression split.
Compare its MAE with the default mean baseline.
slides.note: The median minimizes training absolute loss, but the held-out comparison still needs measurement. Do not promise it always beats the mean on every test sample.

slides.title: Restore the classification partition
points: Use Atr, Ate, btr and bte for this task.
Do not substitute regression arrays because their lengths look familiar.
slides.visual: Regression:Xtr Xte ytr yte;Classification:Atr Ate btr bte
slides.note: The notebook makes separate splits. Names and identities matter more than superficial dimensional similarity.

slides.title: Inspect probability ranges and class order
points: Each binary probability must lie between zero and one.
Confirm which class corresponds to the selected probability column.
slides.note: This check catches mistaken assumptions about column order. It does not establish calibration or deployment reliability.

slides.title: Reproduce the class decisions
points: Use the supplied threshold 0.5 for the reference run.
Compare predicted labels with the classification test targets.
slides.note: Record the actual result. A threshold change is a separate experiment and needs a selection protocol if it supports a final performance claim.

slides.title: Inspect a near-threshold case
points: Find the probability closest to 0.5.
Explain how a small score change could alter its predicted class.
slides.note: Nearness to the chosen threshold is a decision-margin observation. It does not directly quantify epistemic uncertainty.

slides.title: Compare error meaning across tasks
points: A large response error can still have the correct binary sign.
A small error near zero can flip the class.
slides.visual: True response,Predicted response,Effect;10,2,Correct sign but large error;0.1,-0.1,Small error but wrong sign
slides.note: These synthetic examples show why the metrics cannot be ranked by numeric magnitude. The right task depends on the engineering decision.

slides.title: Preserve separate result fields
points: Record Ridge MAE and classification accuracy by name.
Include enough configuration to identify each target and split.
slides.note: Fields should describe what they measure. A generic result field called score can conceal which task and metric were evaluated.

slides.title: Export the actual evidence record
points: Use the notebook's export cell to save the JSON.
Download the notebook and artifacts before ending the runtime.
slides.note: A generated explanation must not substitute invented metrics. Students should be able to trace every result field to a visible execution output.

slides.title: A peer explanation tests understanding
points: Explain the baseline, objective and chosen metric without reading AI text.
State one reason a coefficient is not a causal effect.
slides.note: This rehearsal supports oral assessment. A convincing explanation names mechanisms and assumptions rather than only library functions.

slides.title: Check a real engineering task
points: Would pass/fail inspection need classification or continuous defect severity?
Defend the target using the decision being made.
slides.note: Both tasks can be useful, but they support different decisions. Students should identify what information a binary label discards.

slides.title: The result card separates both claims
points: Report one supported regression claim and one classification claim.
Add the synthetic-data limitation and a proposed external test.
slides.visual: Claim,Task-specific result;Evidence,Actual notebook output;Limit,Synthetic generator;Next test,New sampling condition
slides.note: The final explanation should distinguish algorithm demonstration from deployment validation. The next week studies the evaluation protocol in greater depth.

hours.title: Confusion matrices and decision errors
hours.outcome: Calculate precision, recall, sensitivity and specificity with the correct denominators.
hours.artifact: A complete worked confusion matrix and an error-cost explanation.

slides.title: A decision has two independent labels
points: Ground truth states whether the event actually occurred.
Prediction states the action assigned by the model's decision rule.
slides.visual: Dimension,Possible values;Truth,Event or no event;Decision,Positive or negative
slides.note: A predicted positive does not mean the event is truly present. Separating these two dimensions creates the four possible outcomes.

slides.title: Define the positive event first
points: Here positive means a component truly has a defect.
A positive prediction means the system flags it for inspection.
slides.note: Positive is a coding and decision convention, not a synonym for good. Students should state what class 1 means before computing any metric.

slides.title: Four outcomes form one matrix
points: Rows are actual classes and columns predicted classes.
The order [0,1] produces TN, FP, FN, TP when flattened row-wise.
slides.note: This is a synthetic worked example with 120 components. Repeat the axis convention explicitly because matrix order differs across tools and diagrams.

slides.title: A true positive catches the event
points: The component is defective and receives a positive flag.
In the worked example, TP=15.
slides.note: Explain the two uses of true and positive: true means agreement with the actual class; positive means the declared event class.

slides.title: A false positive raises a false alarm
points: The component is not defective but receives a positive flag.
In the worked example, FP=10.
slides.note: A false alarm can consume inspection time, discard useful material or interrupt production. Its cost depends on the application.

slides.title: A false negative misses the event
points: The component is defective but receives a negative decision.
In the worked example, FN=5.
slides.note: Missed events may be costly, but the course should not invent a universal cost ratio. Ask students to justify costs for a stated engineering context.

slides.title: A true negative correctly clears a case
points: The component is not defective and receives a negative decision.
In the worked example, TN=90.
slides.note: Correct negatives can dominate accuracy when the event is rare. They still matter in the workload and specificity calculations.

slides.title: Totals expose the denominator
points: There are 20 actual defects and 100 actual nondefects.
There are 25 predicted positives and 95 predicted negatives.
slides.note: Verify every total against the matrix. Precision and recall differ because they condition on different sets.

slides.title: Precision conditions on the alarm
points: Of all flagged components, what fraction are defective?
Precision is TP divided by TP+FP.
slides.note: The denominator is the predicted-positive set. Say among flags before presenting the formula to make the conditional meaning explicit.

slides.title: Recall conditions on the real event
points: Of all truly defective components, what fraction were flagged?
Recall is TP divided by TP+FN.
slides.note: The denominator is the actual-positive set. A model can have high recall while flagging many nondefective components.

slides.title: Sensitivity is another name for recall
points: For the declared positive class, sensitivity equals true positive rate.
It is not an additional independent metric.
slides.visual: Recall;Sensitivity;True positive rate;Same denominator: TP + FN
slides.note: Avoid teaching these three names as unrelated measures. The equality depends on keeping the same positive class and population.

slides.title: Specificity conditions on actual negatives
points: Of all nondefective components, what fraction were cleared?
Specificity is TN divided by TN+FP.
slides.note: A specificity of 0.90 means 90 percent of actual negatives are correctly negative. It does not mean 90 percent of negative predictions are correct.

slides.title: False-positive rate complements specificity
points: FPR is FP divided by FP+TN.
With the same negative population, FPR equals 1-specificity.
slides.note: State the complement relationship with its shared denominator. One minus precision is a different quantity conditioned on predicted positives.

slides.title: Accuracy mixes both class populations
points: Accuracy is TP+TN divided by all observations.
The worked example gives 105/120=0.875.
slides.note: Compare with precision 0.60 and recall 0.75. All three are correct yet answer different questions about the same decisions.

slides.title: Rare events can make accuracy deceptive
points: With 5 defects in 100 cases, predicting no defects gets 95 percent accuracy.
That rule has zero recall for defects.
slides.note: Precision is undefined for this no-positive-prediction rule, not inherently zero. Software may report a chosen zero_division convention.

slides.title: F1 balances precision and recall
points: The harmonic mean penalizes a low value in either component.
F1 omits true negatives from its formula.
slides.note: F1 is useful for some objectives but does not encode all costs or true-negative behavior. It should not be presented as universally best.

slides.title: Undefined metrics need an explicit policy
points: Precision has a zero denominator if no case is predicted positive.
Recall has a zero denominator if no actual positive is present.
slides.note: A reporting convention such as zero_division=0 makes software output finite but does not change the underlying mathematical undefinedness.

slides.title: Negative predictive value has another condition
points: Among negative predictions, NPV asks how many are truly negative.
It uses TN divided by TN+FN.
slides.note: Include this to prevent confusion with specificity. The conditioning set is predicted negatives rather than actual negatives.

slides.title: Prevalence affects precision
points: A rarer event can yield fewer true alarms relative to false alarms.
Sensitivity and specificity alone do not determine precision without prevalence.
slides.visual: precision = TPR*pi / (TPR*pi + FPR*(1-pi));pi is event prevalence
slides.note: Explain the formula by expected counts in a population. It assumes the stated conditional rates apply in that population and does not guarantee they survive distribution shift.

slides.title: A prevalence example changes the alarm quality
points: In 1000 cases at 1 percent prevalence, use TPR=0.8 and FPR=0.1.
Expected TP=8 and FP=99 give precision about 0.0748.
slides.note: These are expected synthetic counts under stipulated rates. The example shows why a seemingly good sensitivity can coexist with many false alarms.

slides.title: Error costs connect metrics to action
points: Suppose a false negative costs 20 units and a false positive costs 1.
The worked matrix then incurs 5*20+10*1=110 units.
slides.note: These costs are illustrative, not an empirical industrial estimate. Real costs and capacity constraints must come from the decision context.

slides.title: A threshold changes the alarm set
points: Lowering the threshold adds predicted-positive cases.
Recall cannot decrease on fixed scores, while precision need not change monotonically.
slides.note: The live example holds scores and truths fixed. Require students to predict the effect on TP, FP and FN before moving the threshold.

slides.title: A score and a decision are different
points: The fitted model provides scores or probability estimates.
A threshold translates those scores into actions.
slides.note: A different threshold can produce a different confusion matrix without retraining. Distinguish model evaluation from policy evaluation.

slides.title: Check: which denominator is correct?
points: Among all actual defects asks for recall.
Among all flagged components asks for precision.
slides.note: Ask for the denominator in words first. A student who memorizes the formula but cannot name the population has not mastered the metric.

slides.title: A matrix needs counts as well as ratios
points: Report TP, FP, FN and TN beside the metrics.
Small counts make ratios unstable and uncertain.
slides.note: This revisits the same worked population to connect reporting with uncertainty. It is a deliberate worked-example continuation rather than a new measurement result.

slides.title: The decision requirement precedes optimization
points: Decide which event, errors and operating constraints matter.
Choose evaluation metrics that express those requirements.
slides.note: The hour's artifact is the worked matrix with a short cost rationale. Students must avoid selecting a metric only because it makes their model look good.

hours.title: Validation, overfitting and threshold selection
hours.outcome: Separate fitting, selection and final evaluation without consuming test evidence.
hours.artifact: A validation-only threshold choice and a frozen test protocol.

slides.title: Training and evaluation answer different questions
points: Training measures fit to known examples.
Evaluation estimates behavior on a declared unseen sample.
slides.note: A training score is not useless, but it cannot replace unseen evidence. The gap can provide a diagnostic rather than a final guarantee.

slides.title: Overfitting includes adaptive human choices
points: Repeatedly selecting features against the same held-out score uses that evidence.
Tuning a threshold is also model selection.
slides.visual: Feature choices;Model settings;Threshold choice;Selection overfits evidence
slides.note: The selection process includes the human or AI assistant making changes. Hiding those changes from a parameter list does not preserve test independence.

slides.title: Three partitions separate three jobs
points: Train estimates model parameters.
Validation selects choices before one final test assessment.
slides.note: These are the supplied Week 5 notebook's 800-row partition counts. The class ratio is nominally imbalanced and should be checked from actual generated labels.

slides.title: A clean selection loop excludes test labels
points: Fit candidates on training, then compare them using validation.
Freeze all choices before producing test predictions.
slides.note: Ask where a threshold belongs. It is selected on validation, even if it is not stored inside the estimator object.

slides.title: A reused test set becomes selection evidence
points: Looking at test scores after every edit affects future choices.
Renaming it test does not restore independence.
slides.visual: Candidate 1 test;Edit after score;Candidate 2 test;Adaptive selection
slides.note: Distinguish an honest exploratory analysis from a fresh final evaluation. The solution is a protected evaluation protocol, not pretending the earlier consultation did not happen.

slides.title: Cross-validation rotates validation folds
points: Each fold trains on the remaining folds and validates on the held-out fold.
Preprocessing must be refitted inside each fold.
slides.note: CV provides repeated internal validation under its assumptions. A group or time-aware task requires appropriate fold construction rather than arbitrary shuffling.

slides.title: Fold averages hide variation
points: Report the distribution of fold scores as well as an average when useful.
Correlated folds do not behave like independent new studies.
slides.visual: Schematic fold A:0.70;Schematic fold B:0.76;Schematic fold C:0.73
slides.note: These values are illustrative, not computed CV outputs. Avoid interpreting fold standard deviation as a universal confidence interval for deployment performance.

slides.title: Learning curves separate possible problems
points: Low training error with much higher validation error suggests overfitting.
High errors in both can indicate underfitting or a difficult task.
slides.note: These are qualitative diagnostic shapes, not actual training logs. Distribution shift or flawed splits can also cause a gap.

slides.title: Regularization can reduce flexibility
points: Penalizing large weights changes the bias-variance trade-off.
Improvement must be assessed with selection-safe evidence.
slides.visual: More flexible:Potentially lower train loss;More constrained:Potentially more bias
slides.note: Do not promise that regularization always improves validation error. The effect depends on the task, representation, noise and penalty.

slides.title: A validation grid declares the search
points: Fix candidate thresholds before consulting final test outcomes.
The notebook examines 19 values from 0.05 through 0.95.
slides.visual: thresholds = linspace(0.05, 0.95, 19);Choose using validation F1 only
slides.note: A threshold grid is a hyperparameter search. Even though it seems lightweight, it can overfit validation noise.

slides.title: Select using the stated objective
points: The supplied example chooses the largest validation F1.
This does not establish a universal operational optimum.
slides.note: These three numbers are a small hand-created selection example, not the notebook's output. The selected candidate here is 0.5.

slides.title: Tie handling is part of the rule
points: numpy argmax returns the first maximum in the ordered array.
Record the candidate grid order and the tie policy.
slides.note: For an ascending grid, an exact tie selects the first tied threshold. State the convention rather than suggesting it encodes a scientific preference.

slides.title: The final test assesses the selected rule
points: Apply the chosen threshold to test probabilities once.
Recompute the test confusion counts using that frozen rule.
slides.visual: Chosen validation threshold;Test scores;Frozen decisions;Final counts
slides.note: Test F1 need not match validation F1. Sampling variation and selection bias can cause a difference without implying a software error.

slides.title: Threshold choice can reflect a constraint
points: An application might demand minimum validation recall.
Feasibility, uncertainty and inspection capacity still matter.
slides.visual: Demonstration objective:Max validation F1;Operational objective:Declared cost or constraint
slides.note: This is an alternative protocol, not an instruction to change the supplied notebook silently. A safety requirement needs a defensible statistical treatment.

slides.title: Ranking curves do not choose the action alone
points: ROC uses TPR against FPR across thresholds.
A precision-recall view focuses on alarm quality and event capture.
slides.note: The figure is schematic. Explain how prevalence and operating costs affect interpretation, especially for rare events.

slides.title: Open the Week 5 notebook
points: Use the synthetic 800-row binary classification problem.
Keep the test partition outside threshold selection.
slides.visual: Notebook: week-05-practice.ipynb~Task: imbalanced synthetic classification~Positive class: less frequent event

slides.title: Inspect the nominal imbalance
points: The generator requests weights [0.85,0.15].
Label noise and sampling mean actual counts should be inspected.
slides.note: These are requested proportions, not a claim about exact realized counts. Students should count labels in the generated data and each partition.

slides.title: Reconstruct the 60-20-20 split
points: The first split reserves 40 percent of rows.
The second divides that remainder equally into validation and test.
slides.note: Both splits use stratification in the supplied code. Distinguish count preservation from solving leakage or time-order issues.

slides.title: Fit logistic regression on training
points: Use the supplied maximum-iteration setting.
Validation receives probability estimates from the fitted model.
slides.note: Validation labels appear only in the selection calculation. The fitting path must not include validation or test outcomes.

slides.title: Compute validation F1 for each threshold
points: Turn each threshold into a validation prediction vector.
Compare it with yva, not with yte.
slides.visual: f1_score(yva, pv >= t, zero_division=0)~# Repeat over the predefined grid

slides.title: Plot the selection evidence
points: The x-axis is threshold and the y-axis validation F1.
Mark the threshold chosen by the declared rule.
slides.note: The lecture curve is schematic. The actual plotted scores must come from the student's executed grid.

slides.title: Lock the selected threshold
points: Save the chosen value and grid alongside the model configuration.
Do not update it after viewing test errors.
slides.note: If a test review motivates a new version, evaluate that new version with appropriately fresh evidence. Keep the distinction between exploration and final reporting honest.

slides.title: Compute test probabilities only for assessment
points: Extract test scores from the fitted model.
Apply the frozen threshold without refitting.
slides.note: Predicting test scores does not itself use test labels. The protected boundary concerns selection or fitting influenced by held-out information.

slides.title: Name all four test counts
points: With labels=[0,1], ravel gives TN, FP, FN and TP.
Check that their sum equals 160.
slides.note: The explicit label order makes the shape robust even if one class is absent. Metric denominators can still be zero in other datasets.

slides.title: Explain the selected rule's limitation
points: A best grid value can be sensitive to one validation sample.
Report the search protocol, not just the winning score.
slides.visual: Winning number:One selected threshold;Reproducible evidence:Grid plus split plus objective
slides.note: Students should say why the chosen value is dataset-specific. This is more informative than treating a single threshold as a law.

slides.title: Preserve the H3 checkpoint
points: Save scores, threshold, partition descriptions and observed counts.
H3 will reconcile metrics and inspect failures.
slides.visual: Grid and scores;Frozen threshold;Test counts;Evidence checkpoint
slides.note: Keep validation and test results in distinct labeled fields. A copied screenshot without configuration cannot support a reproducible threshold-selection claim.

slides.title: Restart and run through setup
points: Record the actual runtime and package versions.
Regenerate data in the supplied cell order.
slides.visual: Restart runtime~Run setup~Generate the original synthetic dataset
slides.note: A fixed seed does not compensate for a different sequence of random-number calls. Keep the reference execution order intact.

slides.title: Inspect the partition sizes
points: Confirm 480 training, 160 validation and 160 test rows.
Count class labels within each partition.
slides.note: The size check is exact for the supplied construction. Class counts must come from the actual labels rather than the nominal 15 percent target weight.

slides.title: Verify the declared positive class
points: Explain what class 1 means in this synthetic problem.
Preserve that meaning in every metric and plot.
slides.visual: Positive class:Less frequent generated event;Negative class:Other generated class
slides.note: The synthetic labels do not automatically correspond to a particular clinical or industrial event. Any analogy must be declared rather than treated as data provenance.

points: Trace the model.fit call and its two arguments.
Both arguments must belong to the training partition.
slides.visual: model.fit(Xtr,ytr)~# No Xva or Xte in fitting
slides.note: Students should inspect what the code does, not merely whether its variable names look reassuring. Array provenance determines the actual protocol.

points: Generate the original 19 thresholds.
Compute F1 using validation labels only.

slides.title: Inspect all candidates before the winner
points: View the validation curve and the selected grid position.
Record ties if the maximum occurs at multiple values.
slides.note: The actual grid can have flat regions because changing a threshold does not always cross an observed score. A smooth illustrative curve is not a measured result.

slides.title: Save the threshold before testing
points: Store the chosen threshold with its selection objective.
Include the split seed and candidate grid in the explanation.
