slides.note: The supplied evidence JSON may not contain every audit detail. Preserve missing protocol details in the notebook narrative rather than claiming an export records fields it does not include.

slides.title: Compute a frozen test decision vector
points: Apply the same threshold to all test scores.
Do not adjust it after seeing individual errors.
slides.note: Explain the distinction between inspecting a failure for understanding and using it to retune a final reported model.

slides.title: Sum the four confusion counts
points: TN+FP+FN+TP must equal the number of test observations.
The positive and negative subtotals must match yte.
slides.visual: TN + FP + FN + TP = 160;TP + FN = actual positives;TN + FP = actual negatives
slides.note: This is an arithmetic consistency check. It does not prove the underlying data or labels are correct, but it catches accounting mistakes.

slides.title: Recompute precision manually
points: Divide actual true-positive count by all predicted positives.
State a policy if no case is predicted positive.
slides.visual: precision = TP / (TP + FP);Undefined if TP + FP = 0
slides.note: Match the manual result to the library convention. Reporting zero because of zero_division is different from observing a well-defined ratio equal to zero.

slides.title: Recompute recall and sensitivity
points: Divide true positives by actual positives.
Confirm that both metric names yield the same value.
slides.note: A discrepancy indicates inconsistent class definitions, denominators or implementation. It is not a meaningful difference between two independent measures.

slides.title: Recompute specificity independently
points: Divide true negatives by actual negatives.
Do not substitute TN/(TN+FN).
slides.visual: specificity = TN / (TN + FP);TN / (TN + FN) is NPV
slides.note: Students often confuse specificity and negative predictive value because both involve TN. Name the conditioning set in words to disambiguate them.

slides.title: Recompute F1 from counts
points: Use 2TP divided by 2TP+FP+FN.
Compare it with the precision-recall harmonic mean when defined.
slides.note: The two expressions agree when their relevant denominators permit the calculation. Handle empty or undefined cases transparently.

slides.title: Inspect a false negative if present
points: Find a test case with true label 1 and predicted label 0.
Record its score relative to the chosen threshold.
slides.visual: missed = np.flatnonzero((yte==1) & (~predicted))~# Inspect one only if missed is nonempty
slides.note: If no false negative occurs in this run, report that observation and its limited sample scope. Never fabricate a missed case.

slides.title: Inspect a false positive if present
points: Find a test case with true label 0 and predicted label 1.
Explain why the action is a false alarm.
slides.visual: alarms = np.flatnonzero((yte==0) & predicted)~# Inspect one only if alarms is nonempty
slides.note: The model may score a negative case highly because distributions overlap or features are insufficient. A plausible explanation remains a hypothesis.

slides.title: Compare errors with a declared cost model
points: Choose illustrative FN and FP costs before a new comparison.
Compute cost from the frozen test matrix without changing the rule.
slides.visual: total cost = C_FN*FN + C_FP*FP;Declare units and assumptions
slides.note: This is a cost interpretation of existing outcomes, not a license to optimize costs on the same final test. Any new operating rule needs selection-safe evidence.

slides.title: Explore thresholds without relabeling evidence
points: Use the live synthetic demo to understand the trade-off.
Keep the notebook's final test protocol unchanged.
slides.note: The demo is deliberately separate from the notebook data. It permits free exploration without consuming the notebook's final held-out sample.

slides.title: Selection uncertainty deserves a limitation
points: A small validation set can favor a threshold by chance.
A narrow winning margin may not indicate a stable optimum.
slides.visual: Observed:Best candidate on this split;Unproven:Best threshold in deployment
slides.note: Students can propose repeated internal validation or more data as future work. Do not add a claimed uncertainty interval that has not been calculated.

slides.title: Class shift can alter alarm quality
points: A different event prevalence changes expected precision under fixed conditional rates.
Conditional rates may also shift in a new environment.
slides.note: The prevalence formula is conditional on rate transportability. The real deployment problem may violate that assumption as well.

slides.title: Subgroup errors need counts
points: A subgroup ratio based on few positives can be unstable.
Report the subgroup definition and denominator.
slides.visual: Group,Needed evidence;Machine type,Positive count;Collection site,Negative count;Time period,Sample window
slides.note: This is an extension plan, not a claim that the synthetic notebook contains meaningful demographic or machine subgroups.

slides.title: Export the actual test summary
points: Preserve threshold, confusion counts and metrics from execution.
Download the JSON and notebook before ending the runtime.
slides.note: The supplied export stores observed results. Add explanatory narrative for protocol details that are not included automatically.

slides.title: Check consistency across artifacts
points: The notebook, JSON and report must describe the same run.
Separate validation selection scores from final test metrics.
slides.visual: Notebook execution;JSON summary;Written report;Matching run identity
slides.note: A copied older plot can contradict a new JSON file. Evidence consistency is part of reproducibility, not cosmetic presentation.

slides.title: Explain why accuracy is insufficient here
points: Name the event prevalence and error types that accuracy compresses.
Use the actual confusion counts rather than a slogan.
slides.visual: Accuracy:One aggregate ratio;Decision analysis:Counts and consequences
slides.note: A complete response explains which mistakes matter and how many occur. Saying imbalanced data is bad is too vague.

slides.title: Defend the choice orally
points: Explain why the threshold came from validation.
State one limitation and one concrete follow-up evaluation.
slides.note: This is preparation for written and oral assessment. Students should explain the information boundary without relying on memorized function calls.

slides.title: The report closes the evidence loop
points: Include positive class, split, threshold, counts and metrics.
End with cost assumptions and a restrained claim.

hours.title: Representations and principal components
hours.outcome: Explain PCA as a training-fitted geometric projection with explicit information loss.
hours.artifact: A hand-computed PCA example and an interpretation boundary.

slides.title: Unsupervised learning receives inputs
points: The fitting procedure receives X without target labels.
Discovering structure does not automatically give it semantic meaning.
slides.visual: Supervised:X and y for fitting;Unsupervised:X for fitting
slides.note: The notebook retains hidden generating labels only for optional teaching comparisons. They must not enter the unsupervised fitting path.

slides.title: A representation defines similarity
points: Distance depends on the features, units and transformation.
Changing the representation can change the groups we observe.
slides.note: Ask whether clustering the same objects by mass and color asks the same question. Similarity is a modeling choice, not an intrinsic universal property.

slides.title: A high-dimensional point is one observation
points: Five features place each notebook observation in five-dimensional space.
A two-axis display shows only a projection of that information.
slides.note: The displayed rows are a schematic matrix, not sampled notebook outputs. Students should keep observation count separate from feature dimension.

slides.title: Euclidean distance combines coordinate differences
points: Squared distance sums squared differences over features.
Features with large numerical ranges can dominate it.
slides.note: A dimension with large units can overpower the rest without being physically more important. Scaling encodes an assumption about comparison.

slides.title: Standardization changes the geometry
points: Each feature uses a training mean and scale.
Equalized variance is a modeling choice rather than a physical law.
slides.visual: Raw space:Units set relative influence;Standardized space:Training scales set influence
slides.note: A standardized feature with tiny measurement noise can still be problematic. Domain knowledge should determine whether scaling is appropriate.

slides.title: Unsupervised preprocessing can also leak
points: A scaler or PCA fitted on test rows learns from held-out inputs.
A new-observation evaluation should fit these stages on training only.
slides.visual: Training X;Fit scaler and PCA;Frozen transforms;New X
slides.note: Labels are not required for leakage. Whether a transductive procedure is valid depends on the stated task, which here is held-out transformation and prediction.

slides.title: PCA finds directions of variation
points: The first component maximizes projected training variance under unit length.
Later components are orthogonal directions with remaining variance.
slides.note: PCA is unsupervised because this objective uses X rather than y. Large variation need not be useful for a later target.

slides.title: Centering establishes the origin
points: Subtract the training feature mean before finding directions.
New observations use that same stored mean.
slides.visual: Training mean;Centered training matrix;Principal directions;Frozen projection
slides.note: scikit-learn PCA centers but does not automatically standardize feature variance. The notebook therefore uses a separate StandardScaler first.

slides.title: Covariance summarizes linear co-variation
points: Positive covariance indicates coordinates tend to increase together.
The covariance matrix is symmetric.
slides.note: This stipulated two-feature covariance is an exact worked example, not the computed covariance of the notebook's five-feature dataset.

slides.title: Eigenvectors give principal directions
points: For covariance [[2,1],[1,2]], the first direction is (1,1)/sqrt(2).
Its eigenvalue is 3.
slides.note: Verify the multiplication explicitly. A normalized vector is needed to interpret variance along the direction.

slides.title: The second direction is orthogonal
points: The direction (1,-1)/sqrt(2) has eigenvalue 1.
It is perpendicular to the first principal component.
slides.note: The two directions form an orthonormal basis in this two-dimensional example. The sign of either component can be reversed without changing the subspace.

slides.title: Explained variance is a proportion
points: The first component retains 3/(3+1)=75 percent of variance.
Retaining variance is not classification accuracy.
slides.note: The denominator is total variance in this covariance example. A 75 percent explained-variance ratio does not mean 75 percent correct predictions.

slides.title: Projection computes a coordinate
points: For a centered point (2,0), PC1 score is sqrt(2).
Projection keeps the component along the selected direction.
slides.note: This is one centered observation in the worked two-dimensional geometry. The scalar score is a coordinate in the new basis, not a class label.

slides.title: Reconstruction reveals lost information
points: Reconstructing that point from PC1 alone yields (1,1).
The residual (1,-1) lies in the discarded direction.
slides.note: The squared reconstruction error is 2. This calculation makes information loss concrete instead of presenting dimensionality reduction as free compression.

slides.title: Projection angle changes retained variance
points: Rotate the projection line and inspect the projected spread.
The largest-variance direction defines PC1 for the displayed points.
slides.note: The live demo uses a small explicit synthetic point set, not the notebook's fitted PCA. The displayed angle optimum follows its two-feature covariance.

slides.title: SVD computes the same geometry
points: A centered matrix can be decomposed as U S V-transpose.
Columns of V encode principal directions.
slides.note: The variance relation uses sample covariance. Keep it distinct from StandardScaler's population-variance convention introduced in Week 2.

slides.title: PCA signs can flip harmlessly
points: A component and its negative describe the same axis.
A mirrored scatter plot can preserve identical geometry.
slides.note: A sign flip is not necessarily a reproducibility failure. Compare explained variance and subspaces before concluding that two implementations disagree.

slides.title: Two components can hide separation
points: Points separated in discarded coordinates can overlap in a 2D plot.
Visual overlap does not prove equality in the original feature space.
slides.note: The graphic is schematic and illustrates information loss. The actual notebook fits clustering in the original standardized five-dimensional space.

slides.title: High variance need not be useful signal
points: Lighting or sensor drift can dominate observed variation.
A small-variance direction may carry task-relevant information.
slides.visual: Large variance:Possible nuisance process;Small variance:Possible discriminative signal
slides.note: PCA's objective does not know which scientific mechanism or future target matters. Interpret components with domain evidence.

slides.title: PCA loadings describe directions
points: A loading expresses how an original feature contributes to a component.
Correlated features can contribute together without implying causation.
slides.visual: Component,Illustrative loading pattern;PC1,Length and width together;PC2,Contrast between features
slides.note: These are conceptual loading descriptions rather than the notebook's numerical loadings. Actual values must be read from the fitted PCA object.

slides.title: Explained variance belongs to the fit sample
points: The notebook reports training explained-variance ratios.
Held-out score geometry can differ under distribution shift.
slides.visual: Training fit;Stored components;New-data transform;Potential changed spread
slides.note: Distinguish the estimated training decomposition from a guarantee about all future observations.

slides.title: A scree plot supports a trade-off
points: Inspect variance across ordered components.
Choose dimensionality with the task and information loss in mind.
slides.visual: Illustrative PC1:45;Illustrative PC2:25;Illustrative PC3:15;Illustrative PC4:10;Illustrative PC5:5
slides.note: These illustrative percentages sum to 100 and are not notebook measurements. The purpose is to explain cumulative variance and a compression choice.

slides.title: PCA is sensitive to outliers
points: Extreme observations can influence means and covariance.
Inspect suspicious measurements before interpreting dominant directions.
slides.note: A distant point may be meaningful or erroneous. Do not remove it solely because its presence makes a visualization less tidy.

slides.title: Check: is 90 percent variance 90 percent accuracy?
points: Explained variance measures preserved input spread.
Accuracy requires targets and a prediction decision.
slides.visual: Explained variance:Geometry of X;Accuracy:Agreement with y
slides.note: Expected answer: no. Students should identify that PCA uses no labels and optimizes a different objective.

slides.title: Check: does PCA standardize automatically?
points: PCA centers its input in this implementation.
The separate scaler controls feature-variance normalization.
slides.note: Expected answer: no automatic per-feature standardization by PCA. Explain why the supplied pipeline contains both stages.

slides.title: A projection needs an interpretation boundary
points: State the representation, fitted directions and retained variance.
Add what the plot cannot establish about physical meaning or labels.
slides.visual: Report item,Needed statement;Representation,Standardized inputs;Projection,Two fitted components;Retained variation,Observed training ratio;Limit,No semantic guarantee
slides.note: The hour's evidence is the exact PCA worked calculation and an interpretation statement. H2 adds clustering rather than treating plotted groups as labels.

hours.title: K-means, distances and geometric groups
hours.outcome: Trace K-means updates and distinguish cluster separation from scientific meaning.
hours.artifact: One hand-worked clustering update and a guided notebook checkpoint.

slides.title: Clustering assigns geometric groups
points: A cluster label names a group under a chosen representation and algorithm.
It does not automatically name a physical state or diagnosis.
slides.visual: Cluster ID:Arbitrary algorithm label;Physical category:Requires independent evidence
slides.note: Ask whether renaming cluster 0 as defective establishes a diagnosis. The proposed interpretation requires external validation.

slides.title: K-means uses nearest-centroid assignment
points: Each point joins the closest centroid under squared Euclidean distance.
The chosen number k is an input to the problem.
slides.note: Explain that assigning by squared distance produces the same nearest centroid as Euclidean distance, but the squared objective affects the geometry of optimization.

slides.title: The objective sums within-group dispersion
points: Minimize squared distances from points to assigned centroids.
The objective depends on feature scale.
slides.note: Inertia decreases with more clusters in many settings, so a lower value by itself does not determine a scientifically meaningful number of groups.

slides.title: A one-dimensional example is traceable
points: Use points 0,2,8,10 and initial centroids 0 and 8.
These values define the complete synthetic example.
slides.note: The vertical plotting offset is only for legibility. The clustering distances in this worked example use the single horizontal feature.

slides.title: Assignment compares two distances
points: Points 0 and 2 are closer to centroid 0.
Points 8 and 10 are closer to centroid 8.
slides.note: All comparisons avoid ties. Students should calculate distances before the class reveals the group assignments.

slides.title: The update computes group means
points: The first group's new center is (0+2)/2=1.
The second group's new center is (8+10)/2=9.
slides.note: The mean minimizes squared distances for a fixed assignment. This connects K-means to the squared-loss baseline reasoning from Week 3.

slides.title: The update reduces this objective
points: Initial squared-distance sum is 8.
Updated centers yield a squared-distance sum of 4.
slides.note: Compute each contribution explicitly: initial 0+4+0+4, then 1+1+1+1. These exact numbers are a hand calculation, not software output.

slides.title: Assignment and update alternate
points: Reassign points to the current centers, then recompute means.
Stop when the declared convergence condition is met.
slides.visual: Initialize centers;Nearest-center assignment;Mean update;Repeat or stop
slides.note: Standard K-means can converge to a local solution. A converged iteration is not proof of the globally best clustering or physical correctness.

slides.title: Initialization can change the solution
points: Different starting centers can lead to different local optima.
Multiple initializations compare solutions under the same objective.
slides.visual: Initialization A;Initialization B;Final inertias;Choose lower objective
slides.note: The notebook explicitly sets n_init=10. This improves search coverage but does not guarantee a globally optimal or semantically valid result.

slides.title: Cluster IDs can permute
points: The same partition can be labeled 0,1,2 in a different order.
Compare memberships or aligned groups, not raw label integers alone.
slides.visual: Run A:A=0 B=1 C=2;Run B:A=2 B=0 C=1
slides.note: Label permutation can be harmless. Students should not infer a changed physical state from an arbitrary numeric ID swap.

slides.title: Choosing k changes the question
points: Larger k allows a finer partition of the representation.
It need not reveal a true count of natural categories.
slides.note: The supplied synthetic generator uses three centers and the notebook sets k=3. This is a teaching construction, not a general estimator of nature's category count.

slides.title: Silhouette compares two distance scales
points: a is mean distance to other points in the same cluster.
b is the lowest mean distance to another cluster.
slides.note: Define b as a mean to another cluster, not distance to the nearest centroid. This distinction is essential for a correct explanation.

slides.title: Compute one silhouette value
points: With a=2 and b=8, silhouette is 6/8=0.75.
Positive values indicate closer within-group neighbors in this representation.
slides.note: These stipulated distances illustrate the formula. They are not the silhouette of the earlier four-point example unless its distances happen to produce them.

slides.title: Separation does not prove semantics
points: A high silhouette supports geometric separation under the chosen metric.
It does not establish causal mechanisms or engineering diagnoses.
slides.visual: Representation;Distance separation;Cluster score;External meaning needs evidence
slides.note: Ask what external measurement would support naming one group a material phase. Algorithmic geometry alone cannot supply that evidence.

slides.title: K-means has geometric preferences
points: Squared Euclidean distance favors compact centroid-based groups.
Nonconvex shapes, unequal scales or outliers can produce misleading partitions.
slides.note: The schematic contrasts a curved structure with centroid-based partitions. It is not an executed benchmark or a claim about all datasets.

slides.title: Open the Week 6 notebook
points: Generate 360 observations with five features and three synthetic centers.
Keep hidden_labels out of every fit call.
slides.visual: X, hidden_labels = make_blobs(~    n_samples=360, n_features=5, centers=3, ...)
slides.note: Guided practice begins here. Hidden labels are retained for optional comparisons only and must not become inputs to PCA or K-means.

slides.title: The split creates 270 and 90 rows
points: Fit the scaler on the 270 training rows.
Apply the frozen scaler to the 90 held-out rows.
slides.note: These counts follow the supplied 25 percent split. Although the task is unsupervised, this notebook evaluates transformation and assignment for unseen observations.

slides.title: Standardize before both fitted methods
points: Ztr and Zte share training-fitted scaling parameters.
PCA and K-means each fit on Ztr.
slides.note: There are two fitted branches after standardization. Do not imply K-means receives the two-dimensional PCA output in this notebook.

slides.title: Fit two principal components
points: PCA learns directions from Ztr only.
Transform Zte into the plotted two-dimensional coordinates P.
slides.note: The plotting coordinates describe held-out observations projected through training-fitted directions. The explained-variance ratios refer to the training fit.

slides.title: Fit K-means in five dimensions
points: The notebook fits KMeans on Ztr, not the 2D plotting coordinates.
Predict held-out groups from Zte.
slides.note: This distinction is central. Coloring a PCA plot by cluster IDs does not mean the clustering algorithm operated in that plotted plane.

slides.title: A colored PCA plot is a view
points: Use P for positions and groups for colors.
Overlap in two dimensions can coexist with separation in five.
slides.note: The lecture graphic is schematic. Students must inspect the actual plot and avoid inferring the full clustering geometry from a two-axis display.

slides.title: Compute silhouette in the fitted space
points: The notebook passes Zte and its predicted groups into silhouette_score.
The metric therefore uses standardized five-feature distances.
slides.note: At least two and fewer than n distinct assigned labels are required. A degenerate grouping needs explicit handling rather than a fabricated score.

slides.title: Interpret retained variance separately
points: Sum the two training explained-variance ratios.
Keep this quantity distinct from test silhouette.
slides.visual: Retained variance:Training PCA geometry;Test silhouette:Held-out group separation
slides.note: The metrics have different definitions and sample roles. Their values should not be averaged or compared as interchangeable performance scores.

slides.title: A useful interpretation needs evidence
points: Inspect original feature summaries for each assigned group.
Propose an independent measurement to test a physical interpretation.
slides.visual: Observation,Possible next evidence;Feature contrast,Original units;Group stability,Repeated sampling;Physical meaning,External measurement
slides.note: A cluster name is initially a hypothesis. Students should state what evidence would disconfirm it as well as what would support it.

slides.title: Check: did hidden labels enter fitting?
points: Trace the inputs to scaler, PCA and KMeans fit calls.
Each should receive features without hidden generating labels.
slides.visual: Xtr only;Scaler fit;PCA fit on Ztr;KMeans fit on Ztr
slides.note: A separate label-based teaching comparison can be legitimate if clearly disclosed. It must not be described as label-free fitting if labels actually influenced model choices.

slides.title: Save the representation checkpoint
points: Record scaling, PCA dimension, k, initialization and seed.
H3 will inspect stability, interpretation and evidence export.
slides.note: These settings are part of the reproducible procedure. Runtime state alone is not a durable record of the experiment.

hours.title: Representation and clustering lab
hours.outcome: Reproduce the geometry workflow and test one interpretation without inventing labels.
hours.artifact: Executed notebook, evidence JSON and a representation-aware result card.

slides.title: Restore the two fitted branches
points: PCA supplies plotting coordinates.
K-means supplies groups in standardized five-dimensional space.
slides.visual: Training-standardized data;PCA branch;KMeans branch;Shared held-out observations
slides.note: Draw the branch structure before students resume. This prevents a common mistaken explanation that the displayed PCA plane was the clustering input.

slides.title: Restart the notebook in order
points: Run setup and data generation from a clean runtime.
Keep the reference seed and construction unchanged for the first pass.
slides.note: The task is CPU-friendly and requires no paid API. Reusing the same run order helps preserve the random-generator state.

slides.title: Inspect the observation matrix
points: Confirm 360 rows and five features before splitting.
Treat hidden_labels as teaching metadata rather than model inputs.
slides.visual: print(X.shape)~# Reference construction: (360,5)~# Do not append hidden_labels to X
slides.note: A target accidentally appended as a feature can create circular groups that appear impressively interpretable.

slides.title: Confirm partition sizes
points: The training matrix has 270 rows and the held-out matrix 90.
Preserve feature order across both partitions.
slides.note: The feature count remains constant through scaling. Dimensionality changes only when the PCA branch projects to two components.

slides.title: Fit the scaler only once on training
points: Reuse it for the held-out transform.
Inspect training means and scales for the fitted representation.
slides.note: Do not refit on Xte to force its mean to zero. A difference in held-out statistics may be a property of sampling or shift.

slides.title: PCA centers but does not standardize
points: The supplied scaler precedes PCA.
Explain the separate job performed by each stage.
slides.note: A model pipeline may contain multiple centering operations for sound mathematical reasons. Students should explain the operations rather than remove one by name alone.

slides.title: Fit and inspect two components
points: Read pca.components_ and explained_variance_ratio_.
Verify that there are two projected coordinates per held-out row.
slides.note: Expected shapes are two by five for the directions and 90 by two for the projected held-out observations.

slides.title: Compute retained variance explicitly
points: Sum the two training explained-variance ratios.
State it as a fraction of training variance in the standardized representation.
slides.visual: retained = ratio_PC1 + ratio_PC2;Not a classification accuracy
slides.note: Students should report the observed value from their run. The lecture does not prescribe a numeric result from an unexecuted notebook.

slides.title: Inspect the uncolored projection first
points: Plot PC1 against PC2 without group labels.
Describe visible spread and overlap before naming any clusters.
slides.note: Ask students to use geometric language such as elongated or overlapping. Avoid semantic labels like defective unless external evidence supports them.

slides.title: Fit K-means in the declared space
points: Use Ztr with k=3 and n_init=10.
Preserve the reference random_state.
slides.note: Explicit n_init makes the configuration clear across library versions with different defaults. The setting does not guarantee global optimality.

slides.title: Predict groups for held-out rows
points: Use kmeans.predict(Zte).
The group ID refers to a learned training centroid.
slides.visual: Held-out features;Frozen training scaler;Learned centroids;Assigned group IDs
slides.note: A test observation does not update its assigned centroid in predict. Refit is a different procedure and must be declared if used.

slides.title: Color the projection with those IDs
points: Positions come from P and colors from groups.
Explain the five-dimensional fit versus two-dimensional display.
slides.note: Ask each pair to draw the two branch inputs. A plot can be visually attractive while its interpretation is wrong.

slides.title: Check silhouette's validity conditions
points: Count distinct group IDs in the evaluation sample.
Silhouette needs at least two and fewer than n groups.
slides.note: With a degenerate assignment, report that the silhouette is undefined under these conditions. Do not insert an arbitrary substitute score.

slides.title: Compute the held-out silhouette
points: Use standardized Zte with the assigned groups.
Report the representation and sample count beside the score.
slides.note: A score has no complete meaning without the space and distance definition. Do not compute it in P and describe it as the notebook's five-feature result.

slides.title: Inspect a boundary observation
points: Compare a point's distances to its nearest two centroids.
A small distance gap suggests ambiguous assignment under this geometry.
slides.note: This is an optional diagnostic extension. A small gap is not a calibrated probability or an estimate of a physical transition.

slides.title: Translate a centroid back to feature units
points: Inverse-transform a centroid through the fitted scaler.
Interpret feature summaries before inventing a group name.
slides.note: The resulting values are means represented by the fitted centroids, not necessarily actual observed specimens.

slides.title: Compare groups without relying on ID order
points: Group 0 has no privileged physical meaning.
Align or compare memberships when labels permute across runs.
slides.visual: Same membership:Different numeric IDs possible;Different membership:Substantive grouping change
slides.note: A raw label equality test is sensitive to permutations. A meaningful comparison requires a permutation-aware measure or explicit alignment.

slides.title: Declare one controlled geometry change
points: Change scaling, k or a single construction parameter.
Keep a saved reference run and predict the effect first.
slides.visual: Reference evidence;One planned change;New run;Compare geometry
slides.note: Avoid changing multiple settings to create a preferred picture. The purpose is to identify which assumption changes the observed structure.

slides.title: Removing scaling changes the metric
points: Raw high-variance features gain numerical influence.
Any new grouping describes a different representation.
slides.note: Neither representation is universally correct. Students should defend the choice using measurement meaning and the engineering question.

slides.title: Vary k as a declared extension
points: Compare several predefined k values using training-safe evidence.
More groups can reduce inertia without improving meaning.
slides.visual: Schematic k2 inertia:100;Schematic k3 inertia:70;Schematic k4 inertia:55
slides.note: These are illustrative decreasing objective values. Real candidate results must come from execution and must not be copied from this schematic.

slides.title: Projection loss is visible in reconstruction
points: Inverse-transform projected coordinates and compare with original standardized inputs.
Describe what two components fail to preserve.
slides.note: This optional diagnostic measures a defined representation error. It is not a downstream prediction metric or a physical measurement error by itself.

slides.title: Hidden-label comparisons need disclosure
points: Generating labels may help evaluate the teaching construction.
If they influence model choices, disclose that supervised information entered selection.
slides.note: A workflow can fit without labels yet use labels to select k. Calling the entire procedure fully label-free would then omit part of the selection process.

slides.title: Export the actual two-metric summary
points: Preserve test silhouette and retained training variance under distinct names.
Save configuration details in the notebook narrative.
slides.note: The metrics refer to different populations and quantities. Do not label either simply accuracy.

slides.title: A result card avoids unsupported names
points: Report geometric groups and the chosen representation.
Label proposed physical meanings as hypotheses requiring validation.
slides.visual: Supported,Geometric separation;Unsupported,Automatic physical diagnosis;Needed next,Independent measurement
slides.note: A useful scientific explanation separates what the algorithm computed from the interpretation a human hopes to attach to it.

slides.title: Peer explain-back closes the lab
points: Explain why K-means did not use the plotted PC coordinates.
State one way projection or scaling can mislead an observer.
slides.visual: Fit space:Five standardized features;Display space:Two principal components
slides.note: The expected answer names both branches and the information discarded in projection. This is stronger evidence than a screenshot of colored clusters.

slides.title: A sequence adds an ordering assumption
points: The next week studies observations whose order carries information.
A shuffled tabular representation can discard temporal structure.
slides.note: This is the bridge to sequences, LSTM and attention. Preserve the distinction between unsupervised geometry and models that explicitly represent order.
